summary: Gudusk Elevator Service Company, a Mid-Atlantic elevator maintenance and modernization contractor, is the firm's client. It entered a Distribution Agreement dated March 2, 2026 with Fougos Lift Components, Inc., under which Gudusk resells and installs Fougos FX-series door operators and elevator controllers in Delaware, Maryland, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The folder also holds an Order Form, a Data Processing Addendum covering building-occupant and service-ticket data, and a Parent Guaranty from Fougos Industrial Holdings Corp. backing Fougos's supply and indemnity obligations. It also holds a September 14, 2026 notice letter from Fougos announcing the sale of its FX product line to Lorvant Vertical Services LLC, a competing elevator maintenance company, and the assignment of the agreement to Lorvant. The supervising partner wants an issue-spotting memo before Gudusk responds. Five problems are planted. (1) A five-year auto-renewal with an early, narrow opt-out window. (2) An uncapped data indemnity created by the main agreement's cap carve-out for Section 14 together with the DPA's incorporation into Section 14. (3) A New York law and forum clause in the guaranty against Delaware law and the Court of Chancery in the main agreement. (4) An exclusivity clause that, read with the Order Form's 'Exclusivity Category', bars Gudusk from servicing any non-Fougos vertical transportation equipment. (5) A successor-assignment carve-out that lets Fougos hand the agreement to Gudusk's competitor without consent. The folder also holds two distractors: a press release and a certificate of insurance.

issues.label: automatic renewal
issues.description: Section 3.2 of the Distribution Agreement (D1) renews the agreement automatically for successive Renewal Terms of five years each. It does so unless a party gives non-renewal notice within a single 30-day window that ends 270 days before the end of the then-current term. The Initial Term under Section 3.1 runs three years from the March 2, 2026 Effective Date, so it ends March 1, 2029. The opt-out window therefore closes roughly nine months before expiry, in early June 2028. A missed window locks Gudusk into five more years of exclusivity and purchase commitments. That lock-in matters more because Fougos has announced, in its September 14, 2026 letter (D3), that it intends to assign the agreement to a competitor.
issues.expected_finding: Section 3.2 auto-renews the agreement for five-year terms unless Gudusk gives notice within a 30-day window closing 270 days before expiry (around early June 2028 for the March 1, 2029 Initial Term end), so the renewal term should be shortened to one year and the window widened to any time up to 90 days before expiry.

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: Section 12.1 of the Distribution Agreement (D1) caps each party's liability at amounts paid or payable in the prior 12 months. Section 12.2 excludes from that cap liability arising under Section 14 (Confidentiality and Data Protection). Read alone, that is an ordinary mutual carve-out for confidentiality breaches. Section 2.1 of the Data Processing Addendum (D4) states that the Addendum is incorporated into Section 14 of the Agreement. Section 9.2 of the Addendum then requires Gudusk alone to indemnify, defend and hold harmless Fougos against all losses, regulatory fines and third-party claims arising from any security incident affecting personal data in Gudusk's systems or service-ticket platforms. Section 11 of the Addendum makes it 'subject to the limitations and exclusions of liability in Section 12 of the Agreement', which looks protective. Through that cross-reference, however, the Section 12.2 exclusion reaches the DPA indemnity. The order of precedence (D1 Section 19.4) cures nothing, because the two documents are consistent with each other. Together the provisions leave Gudusk's data-incident indemnity entirely uncapped.
detect_terms: shall not apply to liability arising under Section 14
issues.expected_finding: Because DPA Section 2.1 incorporates the Addendum into Section 14 of the Distribution Agreement and Section 12.2 removes Section 14 liability from the 12-month fee cap, Gudusk's one-way data-incident indemnity under DPA Section 9.2 is unlimited, so the carve-out should exclude the DPA indemnity or the DPA should carry its own cap (for example a fixed multiple of annual fees).

indemnify, defend and hold harmless Supplier

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: Section 18 of the Distribution Agreement (D1) chooses Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the Delaware Court of Chancery. Section 8 of the Parent Guaranty (D5) applies New York law and submits disputes to the state and federal courts located in New York County. In the guaranty, Fougos Industrial Holdings Corp. guarantees Fougos's supply, warranty and indemnity obligations to Gudusk. Each clause is ordinary on its own. The Distribution Agreement's order of precedence (D1 Section 19.4) covers only the Agreement, the Addendum and the Order Form. The guarantor is not a party to it, so it does not reach the guaranty. To enforce its credit support, Gudusk must therefore litigate the underlying breach in Delaware and the guaranty claim in New York, under different law. That split risks inconsistent rulings and lets the guarantor contest liability already established in Chancery. The split matters more given the assignment announced in the September 14, 2026 letter (D3).
detect_terms: laws of the State of Delaware
Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware
issues.expected_finding: The Parent Guaranty's New York law and New York County forum conflict with the Distribution Agreement's Delaware law and exclusive Court of Chancery forum, and the Agreement's precedence clause does not bind the guarantor, so Gudusk faces split litigation over the same default and should require the guaranty to adopt Delaware law and the Court of Chancery.

issues.label: overbroad exclusivity
issues.description: Section 2.3 of the Distribution Agreement (D1) provides that during the Term, Distributor shall not purchase, sell, install, maintain or service any product within the Exclusivity Category in the Territory other than Supplier's products. Read alone, this is a conventional exclusivity tied to a defined category. Section 1 of the Order Form (D2) limits the Products to Fougos FX-series door operators and controllers. Section 4 of the Order Form, however, sets the Exclusivity Category as 'all vertical transportation products and services'. Read together, the two provisions bar Gudusk from installing or servicing any non-Fougos elevator or escalator equipment anywhere in the four-state Territory. That covers ropes, machines, cabs, fixtures and other manufacturers' controllers, which is essentially Gudusk's whole maintenance business. The deal requires exclusivity only for door operators and controllers. The order of precedence does not cure the problem, because the Order Form definition supplements rather than conflicts with Section 2.3.
issues.expected_finding: Read with the Order Form's definition of the Exclusivity Category as all vertical transportation products and services, Section 2.3 bars Gudusk from installing or servicing any non-Fougos elevator equipment in the Territory, far beyond the FX door operators and controllers actually distributed, so the Exclusivity Category should be redefined as door operators and controllers competitive with the Products and the restriction limited to their sale and installation.
detect_terms2: all vertical transportation products and services

issues.label: unrestricted assignment
issues.description: Section 16.1 of the Distribution Agreement (D1) generally requires consent to assign. Section 16.2 then lets either party assign the agreement to a Permitted Successor without the consent of the other party. Section 1.1 defines Permitted Successor as any person that acquires all or substantially all of the assets of a party's business or of any product line to which this Agreement relates. The definition does not exclude competitors and imposes no creditworthiness or confidentiality conditions. The clause is mutual, but it hurts Gudusk in practice. Because a single product line counts, Fougos can carve out the FX line and transfer the agreement on its own. The September 14, 2026 notice letter (D3) records exactly that: Fougos plans to sell the FX product line to Lorvant Vertical Services LLC, a competing elevator maintenance company, and to assign the agreement to it. Lorvant would then receive Gudusk's pricing, its order history and, through the Data Processing Addendum, Gudusk's customer and building data. The letter also asserts that no consent is required.
detect_terms: without the consent of the other party
any product line to which this Agreement relates
issues.expected_finding: Sections 16.2 and 1.1 let Fougos assign the agreement without Gudusk's consent to anyone acquiring just the FX product line, which the September 14, 2026 notice letter shows it intends to do in favour of competitor Lorvant Vertical Services LLC, so Gudusk should object and require consent for any assignment to a competitor, with a termination right if the agreement is assigned to one.
